text_fidelity_a:
Geeni Sentry Wi-Fi Wireless Smart Floodlight Security Camera, 2-Way Audio, Motion Sensor Alarm, Audio Video Recording, Works with Alexa and Hey Google I ordered the 'Geeni, Sentry Floodlight Security Camera with Motion Sensor, Intruder Alarm and Audio Video Recording' for review and would like to share my thoughts.

So I have had this camera for a while now and finally got it installed a couple of weeks ago and I am ready to share my thoughts and experience so far. This camera requires hard wiring which is why it took so long to get it installed. In my old home it was going to require me to get an extension cord, drill through my wall in the garage and plug it in, in the garage. This was much more work than I had anticipated. Now the new home already had normal motion sensor lights installed on switches, which made this more feasible for me to install. I took one of the motion sensor lights down and had to retrofit a new mount out of a piece of wood to cover the original hole left by removing the old light. This wasn't to hard to do and the Geeni light mounted with ease. Once installed and I turned the light switch on, it was ready to set up which took some time to do. I had to reset the device several times to get the App to set it up properly which was a quite pain however.

The camera itself is very good but so far I am not happy with all the notifications that I get which seem to be false alerts. It seems that everything seems to trigger this thing with absolutely no control as to how sensitive you would like the sensor to be. This is truly my main con with this device. I ended up turning notifications off on my mobile device which kind of defeats the purpose really.

Then there is the App which has thus far been pretty buggy. It has crashed many times and it is not so easy to find the "actual" activity that it seems to detect. Of all the motion activity that it detects, I would say that only 40% of it is relative. I do have the App set to just record everything (continuous) on the 128gb SD card which makes more sense seeing as there are so many false readings.

As for the good of this Geeni device, the image quality both during daytime and nighttime recording and playback is great. There is very little lag when accessing the footage which is surprising as I have other WiFi cameras that are painfully slow to connect and playback footage. This is probably my favorite feature (when the App doesn't crash).

Overall I do like this motion sensor and think that there is absolute value to it. I am however, really hoping for a firmware update which might help with some of the issues and allow you to adjust the sensitivity of the motion detection. Also it would be nice to have an easier way to track down and view "actual" activity rather than having to try and find that exact moment of capture. It seems to just tag a portion of footage, and you need to watch several minutes before you can find what it detected. You are also able to save the footage via the App, but doing so can take several days for it to show up on your mobile device which is another downside to this device.

I hope that this was helpful.
text_fidelity_b: Geeni Sentry Wi-Fi Wireless Smart Floodlight Security Camera, 2-Way Audio, Motion Sensor Alarm, Audio Video Recording, Works with Alexa and Hey Google

text_fidelity_a:
Logitech G933 Artemis Spectrum – Wireless RGB 7.1 Dolby and DTS Headphone Surround Sound Gaming Headset – PC, PS4, Xbox One, Switch, and Mobile Compatible – Advanced Audio Drivers – Black I got this headset during the 50% off deal and I am really enjoying it with Battlefield 5. I decided to upgrade from my Logitech G430 headset. I was mainly looking for a wireless headset that had great battery life, great sound and did not cost too much. Even without the deal, the $200 price point is still reasonable compared to other wireless headsets. I was considering the Corsair and Astro's before purchasing this one. I am using this headset for my PC only, to game.

The Headset:
- Customizable buttons to change the Equalizer, play/pause, and many other options to choose from
- Convenient volume dial to change sound on the fly. This is great so you dont have to minimize the game and adjust the volume settings with the mouse
- Headset grips my head. I have an angled forehead which my old headset would easily slide off when moving around
- Comfy ear pieces that does not cram my ears and feel uncomfortable
- Comes with long braided charging cable, AUX cables, and RCA cables
- USB adapter to connect the wireless headset it plug and play. You just need to make sure you install the Logitech dashboard to customize the headset
- The Logitech logo and a line down each ear-cuff lights up. To me this is a pointless feature as I am wearing the headset and cannot see the lighting and only uses up battery life. I disabled the lights and my battery life increased by 3 hours.

Sound:
The sound i will say is significantly better than my G430. There are multiple equalizer profiles to choose from (FPS, Cinema, etc.). Once you turn on surround sound and 7.1, it makes a big difference of sounds. You can change the treble, bass, and customize the sound to your liking.

Battery:
I cannot say too much about the battery life, but after a full charge, and turning off the leds on the headset. It said I have 12 hours of battery left. After wearing the headset playing Battlefield 5 for 4 hours, I still had 93% battery life. Overtime with charges and draining, i would assume the life would degrade a bit and would get around 10 hours of battery. I did not check how long it takes to charge the headset from a full depletion.

The only cons I have are the pointless LED lights if you are not showing off your headset. I do feel the headband part of the headset is not as strong as I would have expected it to be, just do not twist headband much.
text_fidelity_b: Logitech G933 Artemis Spectrum – Wireless RGB 7.1 Dolby and DTS Headphone Surround Sound Gaming Headset – PC, PS4, Xbox One, Switch, and Mobile Compatible – Advanced Audio Drivers – Black

text_fidelity_a:
Sony ICF-506 Analog Tuning Portable FM/AM Radio, Black, 2.14 lb Growing up I always had a radio in my room. Times are a little different now and I tend to get my music from the Internet, but there are still times when local radio stations are a better choice - particularly during power outages or when getting local news. I have had very good fortune with Sony electronics and computers in the past so I was eager to try this AM/FM tuner and had high expectations. It did not disappoint me.

Let me very clear about this unit - it is for AM/FM receiving only. It does not play MP3’s, it doesn’t play CDs and it doesn’t stream from the Internet. It’s just an AM/FM tuner. It does this quite well, though - better than most other tuners I have used in the last several years.

Right out of the box, this unit looks nostalgic. It has a classic AM/FM radio look and feel, very similar to a radio my father used to have in his workshop when I was a kid. This is a big plus for me, just for the fact that it takes me back to my childhood.

I plugged it in and turned it on, and I immediately tuned to one of the [relatively] local stations. It picked it up and played it very clearly, better than most other tuners I have used in the last 4-5 years. It is definitely better than the car’s radio. I “surfed” the dial and found other stations that I have listened to in the past but thought were out of range and this little radio did a good job of picking them up and playing with minimal static. That’s really all I could ask. It’s not a miracle radio though and it cannot pick up FM stations hundreds of miles away, but it has better range than most I have used recently.

I like that it can be used on AC power or on batteries. That will be handy during weather events.

I can’t find any real reason to complain about this tuner. It works great and looks great too. It is a little on the pricey side which is par for the course for Sony electronics, but it is a fine tuner that is worth its asking price.
text_fidelity_b: Sony ICF-506 Analog Tuning Portable FM/AM Radio, Black, 2.14 lb

LeadsaiL Wireless Computer Mouse, 2.4G Portable Slim Cordless Mouse Less Noise for Laptop Optical Mouse with 4 Buttons, AA Battery Used, USB Mouse for Laptop, Desktop, MacBook Great shape, very much like the classic and ubiquitous Logitech. I like that the pairing device is on-board. Lightweight and simple, a mouse is important for me if needing to get serious work done, especially anything with CAD or Visio.

The big question you need to ask yourself is, do you want a Bluetooth version or one like this that has its own receiver. It seems to me that if you always use this with the same computer and you have Bluetooth built in to the computer, then you probably want Bluetooth. Conversely, if you want this to use with multiple computers and/or you don't have Bluetooth built in to any one of the computers you will use the mouse with, then you'd want something like this. This is because pairing is easier in a case such as this, and drivers usually aren't an issue. Bluetooth usually isn't an issue either, but it might get irritating with frequent changing of machines. At least that is my experience.

Does not come with a carry bag, surprisingly. Mouse roller also functions as a button, as it should. It has an on/off switch on the back, which is nice for saving battery life and being able to leave this hooked up to a permanent install (although with a permanent desk setup, I personally stick with wired).

text_fidelity_a:
ClearClick HD Video Capture Box Ultimate (4K Edition) - Record and Stream Video from HDMI (Up to 4K30) and AV Video Sources - No Computer Required THE GOOD:
--------------
* It will do as it says.. capture videos from your sources.
* Video quality seems fine to me. I'm not that picky, the stuff I record isn't important.
* You can install a micro SD card, or connect a hard drive via usb.

THE BAD:
-----------
* Consistent with their products, they cut corners when it comes to the remote control. It's just a terrible clunky experience. I can't even put into words what's wrong with it. I guess there is a delay. So if you're impatient, you'll be pressing too many buttons, and you'll be in the wrong menu, navigate to the wrong places, enable the wrong features, etc. So my advice is to be patient. Press the button you want to press, then wait a week for it to respond. I don't know what inner components make a great remote control. Whatever they are, they are not inside ClearClick remotes. I've reviewed some of their other Clearclick products that are $150 and less, and so I was more forgiving. But at $250, really? You're going to still skimp out on the remote at this price range?

* If you toggle into PLAYBACK mode... good luck getting out of it. Back button doesn't work, and it's always thinking you want to delete files. Everytime I escape playback mode, I'm relieved, but also have no clue how I got out.

* Power on/off is weird. There are scenarios that will make your heart stop because you'll think the device shorted out. Just like their terrible remotes, I've noticed this power issue with their other models too. The quirk is this... sometimes when you power off and on too quickly, it just goes dead. It will not respond for a long time. Don't panic. Stop pushing the power button. Just unplug everything. The hard drive, the HDMI, the power, unplug everything. Go walk your dog, and when you come back, and connect everything again, it will power up. This happens to other Clearclick devices I have, so when it happened with this device, I didn't panic. I knew what was up.

* Power port is micro usb. Again, at $250, I'd like to see USB-C. Micro usb is antiquated, and their cords are prone to get damaged.

* You will need a HDMI splitter to bypass HDCP, as well as be able to turn off your Clearclick when you're not recording, and still watch TV. In my scenario... my source goes into my splitter, and my splitter has TWO outs. One goes into the Clearclick, and the other goes to my projector. This way, I can turn off my Clearclick if I'm not recording, and still watch my projector. If I connect the source directly to the Clearclick, and then go OUT from the Clearclick to my projector, then I would get their ugly icons on my projector. In my pictures, the source is my Nvidia Shield, you'll notice a row of white icons at the top. There is no option to hide these icons in passthrough mode. So if you use the Clearclick as a passthrough, you will get those ugly icons on your big screen. So even if you're recording sources that do not need a HDMI splitter. I'd still get one anyway because using the hdmi passthrough is not pretty. However, the good thing is that the files you record, will not have those icons.

In conclusion, if this weren't a Vine item, I would send it back. Having said all that, it's possible that my expectations may be unreasonable for a very niche product. If a big company like Sony or Samsung create a polished standalone capture device like this, maybe it'd be $500-$600. In which case, you'd be pretty happy with the ClearClick. If you learn to live with the quirks, it's a nifty piece of tech. Hopefully, they can improve on the user experience through firmware updates. I'll go 3-Stars this time.
text_fidelity_b: ClearClick HD Video Capture Box Ultimate (4K Edition) - Record and Stream Video from HDMI (Up to 4K30) and AV Video Sources - No Computer Required

ClearStream Micron-R Indoor HDTV Antenna with Reflector - 35 Mile Range I have a roof-top antenna that worked well for analog stations but, when I converted to digital, I went from receiving 8 stations to just 1. After trying a few other antennas, I came across the ClearStream 4. I'm able to pull in 20+ digital stations perfectly, and 4 more so-so. Several analog stations come in as well, but the picture is not nearly as good as the digitial stations.

The antenna is well-made, but is a bit of a pain to assemble - lots of pieces to screw together. It only takes about 10 minutes, but you'll probably need to utter a few choice words since it's hard to get the screws to line up properly. The directions are pretty spotty, but give you the essential information. The brackets are heavy-duty, and everything is either aluminum or plastic, so it should hold up well to the elements if I put it outside. Right now, it is in my attic, and may stay there since it pulls in all the stations I want to watch. It does not come with a cable.

It's pretty compact given its performance, and much more compact that the DB8 (another Antenna Direct model with about the same specifications). Very happy with the performance. Also have a DB2 -- see my comments on that review that compare it to this antenna in terms of performance.

text_fidelity_a:
ByronStatics Record Player, Vinyl Turntable Records Player Bluetooth 5.0, Built in Stereo Speakers, 3 Speed, Extra Stylus, Supports RCA Line Out, AUX in, Portable Suitcase Record Player - Dark Grey I had high hopes for this little turntable. It looked perfect for my oldest son who is a huge 80's music fan and thought he should hear it in its original format. We were excited to unbox it and play the two albums we picked up at the used book store. First impressions were OK. The case looks nice and love the two speakers built in. Opening it, we were underwhelmed by the plastic turntable, stylus arm and rather cheap looking controls. But we were still excited.

The sound was also a little disappointing. The two speakers are underpowered and all high end so it was pretty tinny. But the absolute worst was that they stylus is so head light that it skipped constantly. We put a small glass bead on it and the weight actually slowed the turntable. We backed off and placed a quarter on it and it played about right. But again, I was underwhelmed by the underpowered turntable. Also, we noted that one of the spongy pads on the turn table was not installed properly and put a list to the album. We fixed that and fixed the quarter to the stylus and we were able to get it to play through Adam Ant's Friend or Foe album. The scratchy quality of between songs brought me back 40 years to my own first phonograph, which I think was pretty crappy, but probably better than this one.

It works, its nostalgic. We have had fun and will probably get an album at every used bookstore, garage sale, or antique store we find them in, but we will need to upgrade if he goes beyond just enjoying the novelty of it.
text_fidelity_b: ByronStatics Record Player, Vinyl Turntable Records Player Bluetooth 5.0, Built in Stereo Speakers, 3 Speed, Extra Stylus, Supports RCA Line Out, AUX in, Portable Suitcase Record Player - Dark Grey

text_fidelity_a: Apple iPod Touch (4th Generation) Old Model I already own an iTouch 16GB 1st gen. It still works well but I needed more storage for my ever growing TV show and movie collection. I bought mine overseas at a military store that could not keep these in stock. My first thought was how thin it was compared to my old iTouch, nearly half the size. But, recent technology has packed so much more into this small case. I didn't read the specs. I already knew most of what it was supposed to do. I did not know about the external speakers, which sound fine if you make some adjustments. I've watched Blackadder's Christmas Carol and the clarity was amazing. I took some pictures and I don't really like the stills because they seem blurred. The video camera, however, is great. I downloaded the Kindle reader app and was able to sync my existing library. It's nice to see my bookcovers in color and reading the written page is clear and easy on the eyes. The iBooks app is also nice for reading PDFs. Getting online was really quick after locating the nearest free Wi-Fi signal. I use my iTouch mainly for listening to Audible audiobooks, of which I have a massive collection. Because of its size, it is truly more mobile and easier to carry than my Sony Touch ereader, and I don't need additional light to read the screen. Only my netbook gives me more entertainment options because it have much more storage and an external keyboard. The virtual keyboard is small and does the job for typing in website addresses. I would rather use the voice recorder to take notes. I do have a capacative stylus to avoid fingerprints but I will get a screen protector soon. Overall, I paid full price in case I needed to return it for problems. So far, it's been a good deal.
text_fidelity_b: Apple iPod Touch (4th Generation) Old Model

text_fidelity_a:
Koss SP540 Full Size Dynamic Headphones, Black with Silver Accents KOSS has created the perfect headphones for the amateur artist or the casual listener. They have put a great deal of work into both the functionality and aesthetics of this product. There are several things that I noticed at first glance:
(1) Aesthetics: The carrying case for the headphones is attractive. It is thin and practical. It fits well in a book bag, purse or travel bag. It does not take up a lot of room in whatever you chose to carry it in. The headphones fit inside the case nicely (face down), and there is a zippered pouch inside that holds the removable cord. The headphones themselves are sleek looking and attractive. They are black with just a splash of silver.
(2) Cool Feature: Making the cord removable was a great feature. Why? If you ever get a short in the cord, you have the option of simply ordering another cord without having to replace the entire unit. The length of the cord is fantastic....not too long, not too short. The only things that I would probably change about these headphones (although it doesn't affect my love of the product) is to include a volume control button and make the cord a little more decorative (maybe add a nice stripe of red..or something to add some bling). Ok that is just the girl in me.
(3) Fit: The ear muffs (or headphones) fit snuggly over the entire ear. They are nicely padded and comfortable. They do NOT cause irritation from prolonged use or press against the ear causing any discomfort.
(4) Sound quality: The sound quality of the KOSS is great or comparable, especially when I compare it to other sets that I have had in the past. They aren't bass heavy like Beats, but offer decent sound quality like Sennheiser, V-Moda or Sony. The balance and frequency response are good. No matter the type of music.. from Alternative, to Neo Soul, Jazz, Classical to Rock....I get great sound. I am very impressed by the quality.

And finally I will mention:
(5) Cost. This headset will cost you about $150, which is comparable to other headphones of this quality. I truly believe for the money, you are getting a pretty great buy. The sound quality and features make this a great set of headphones for those in the market to consider. You definitely get a lot of bang for your buck. 5 stars
text_fidelity_b: Koss SP540 Full Size Dynamic Headphones, Black with Silver Accents

Fixcracked for iPad mini & iPad mini 2 9.7 inch Touch Screen Replacement Parts Digitizer Glass Assembly+ Professional Tool Kit (black) The gist: the kit is about 85% complete, the glass is easy to install, and it all works well.

I'd almost give this kit 5 stars except for a few salient omissions: the lack of instructions, and a couple of parts which I think should have been included.

There are no instructions included in the kit, and the ones in this listing are garbage. Look to other sources for how to replace the digitizer.

Everything that is included is of adequate quality, and everything was useful. I needed to provide a heat gun and safety glasses (do wear safety glasses, prescription glasses would work just as well, or a face shield--i had little pieces of glass pinging me in the face as I removed the very cracked digitizer).

All told the replacement took me 3 hours to complete. I followed instructions on the iFixit site; there were a few discrepancies but fairly trivial ones, and it included many tips, cautions, and comments, in addition to the directions, that were more than adequate to make the repair fairly easy. As I mentioned, the glass was a mess of cracks, I covered the screen with a couple of layers of packaging tape to hold the majority of shards together as I worked. Once the glass was off everything went pretty smoothly.

The two things which I think should have been included are adhesive and gloves. The glass is taped down, and at least in my case, the tape is almost impossible to recover. The gloves would make keeping the screen and glass free of finger prints. Both would be pretty cheap.
text_fidelity_b: Fixcracked for iPad mini & iPad mini 2 9.7 inch Touch Screen Replacement Parts Digitizer Glass Assembly+ Professional Tool Kit (black)

text_fidelity_a:
Kindle Keyboard, Wi-Fi, 6" E Ink Display - includes Special Offers & Sponsored Screensavers I had decided I did not "need" a Kindle, having tons of other gadgets for all sorts of things. Then I began to lose the vision in one eye and realized over a period of weeks that I could not read normally (or at all some days). Magazines, books, the newspaper.... heck even email was difficult to impossible some days. All my friends have Kindles, so I borrowed one for a day and fell in love. We immediately ordered the Special Offers Wi-Fi Keyboard version. I've had it about 45 days now and my quality of life has seriously improved! I can enlarge the font and change the style of the font depending on my needs at that moment and on really bad days, when my eyes are tired or refusing to focus, the voice function is amazing. The very idea that it reads aloud to me is tremendous and once you adjust to the sometimes robotic pronounciation of some words, it works like a charm. So far, all the books I've purchased have allowed the voice option.

I signed up for Audible.com about two weeks after getting the Kindle and the quality of the audio books on my Kindle is excellent. No robotic voice here - you get the narration exactly as read by the real person - it's an MP3 file I think. Additionally, getting the local newspaper every morning on my Kindle has returned to me my morning tradition of the local editorials & coffee. I do love the number of free books available as well - some are garbage, but most are pretty decent and some have been excellent books. (Loads of Sc-Fi for free too, what's not to love?) I have used the sample option for a ton of books and it's helped me decide to spend the money purchasing a novel, or not. In case you are worried about the Special Offers... they are the screensavers while the Kindle is in sleep mode and NEVER show up in your actual books. I've used a couple of them already now that I think about it.

One last thing - the Kindle in a case, fits into almost all of my handbags and has saved my sanity sitting in doctor's office waiting rooms and at the car repair shop, and I can now sit out under a tree on a pretty day with my horses again while I read a great book. This version of the Kindle will also play my own music while I'm reading. Bottom line is that the Kindle has helped me get a valuable part of my life back and this in turn has allowed me to be more rational while facing possible permanent loss of vision in one eye. Very worthwhile purchase!
text_fidelity_b: Kindle Keyboard, Wi-Fi, 6" E Ink Display - includes Special Offers & Sponsored Screensavers

It produces more than ample volume for most any setting and has several connection methods.

While I have tested and reviewed Bluetooth speakers costing ten times (and more) what this does, the sound quality from this speaker is really quite good. In relation to the sound quality I would place them on par with mid to high end Bluetooth speakers.

In regards to charging time and battery life, both are outstanding. In my tests charging takes about approximately 2 hours to charge the built in 4000 mAh battery and the speaker lasts a solid 4.5 hours at max volume - 8 hour with volume midway (of course this will vary a bit due to exact settings).

There are multiple ways to connect to this speaker including Bluetooth 5.0, which can reach much further than previous versions, through an AUX cable, a 3.5mm jack, TF card, USB flash drive, or FM radio - it even has a built in extendable antenna.

While it has a remote and I tested it and it works fine, I rarely use it as I connect with my phone all the time.

I have taken this speaker with me to the pool for the last couple of months and have been thoroughly impressed with its performance. The battery, being 4000 mAh, is much longer lasting than most allowing for all day listening and the sound quality has been really good.

This is an all around great Bluetooth speaker that I certainly recommend.

I got the black one so it sits very nicely behind a few Knick Knacks and not really visible. The sound is "surround" so it's not directional. I have not paired it up with a twin to test out the stereo effect. But that's not how I intend to use this speaker anyways.

There is also a web page where you can sign in and view your cameras when you're away from home. Best of all, there's an iphone app that also lets you check your cameras. Just viewing is free, if you want the deluxe versions that allow you to change camera setting remotely there is an additional fee. Just viewing is sufficient for my needs however.

One annoyance I've found so far is there are FOUR different colored very bright (some flash) LEDs on the power unit for the main camera. It's VERY annoying and attention grabbing, and screams "UNPLUG ME!" You can turn off the LEDs on the camera itself (I don't, love the deterrent) but there is no way to disable them on the power box. I have a wireless media remote keyboard that I used to use with an HTPC that needs a USB dongle, and wanted to also take advantage of the wired Ethernet jack I had previously installed by my TV (wired is always more reliable for streaming in our experience). This device seemed perfect! It connects to the power socket of the Fire stick and offers a USB hub with ethernet jack.
The problem is, the ethernet jack doesn't seem to be recognized by the Firestick at all! I know what it is supposed to do when it recognizes a network jack, but the option to use the wired internet simply doesn't show up- it doesn't know or acknowledge it is there!
On the upside, at least the USB sockets work, so I was able to use my media remote keyboard. In fact, this device comes in two parts- one is a USB host plug that allows a single USB connection while passing power, and a standard USB hub + ethernet that attaches to that. In all honestly, if I just want to use the USB media remote, I don't need the hub... I can plug it directly into the host port without the hub attached. Its a shame because I really want ethernet. So it only half works.

TP-Link AV2000 Powerline Adapter - 2 Gigabit Ports, Plug&Play(TL-PA9020 KIT),White I was expecting a bigger performance bump with the MIMO technology. I have been using TP-Link AV1200 3 ports with electric outlet pass throughs, but I was willing to lose the outlets and one port for better performance. It is a bit better - and the powerline upstairs is in an area that gets zero wifi connectivity - but we are still talking 15-20 Mbps, where I get well over 100 on my wifi downstairs.

I'm not convinced that this is the fault of the product. The rooms are all on different circuits - sometimes different circuits within the same room. It's not an optimal situation for powerline connections. If you have a wifi dead spot in a place where you need internet, I think this technology is worth a try. I bought my 3-port models with the pass-through not too long ago and am happy with them. These are enough faster that my son might want me to use them instead.

It is bulky and awkward to wear, but does have a hip belt to take the weight off the shoulders. Also, I tried a holster style case, but it never felt secure and I never trusted my camera and lense in such a flimsy case. The sling, once in place seems to become a part of my body while hiking and climbing. It feels more secure than the backpack and far more secure than the holster.

Good Points

- nice spacious compartment for a DSLR and Zoom lense
- Sturdy with strap across you chest, it feels very secure on.
- Rotating the sling gives a sturdy platform to remove or insert camera.
- It is not big enough to overpack
- plenty of space for battery, charger, cards, notebook or guide, and two lenses and body
- Rain cover is nice addition (have not used it, but love the extra insurance.)
- Well padded
- Nice construction, classic design.
- Nice side handle for carrying when not slung.

Bad Points

- Sling Accentuates Man-boobs (I've tried several different ways of placing the strap, but it seems the only fix is portion control and moderate exercise.)
- no hip belt so weight is held on shoulders for long hikes, but weight is limited somewhat by size.

All in all, I have to admit I have come to love this sling. It has traveled with me quite a bit and I trust it to hold my treasured camera and lense. Easy to pack and will handle the essentials. It is cheaper than the Lowe sling in price, but not functionality. I recommend this to anyone who wants to pack in a DSLR.

text_fidelity_a:
OhO Audio Sunglasses,Open Ear Audio Sunglasses Speaker to Listen Music and Make Phone Calls,Water Resistance and Full UV Lens Protection for Outdoor Sports and Compatiable for All Smart Phones Let's get one thing straight right away: THESE ARE NOT SUNGLASSES. They are blue-light blocking at best, or just mildly tinted most likely. I took them out of the box and thought "Oh cool! These are the kinds of glasses that get dark outside and transparent when you are inside!", but nope- I wore them for a full hour outside and they didn't get any darker or exhibit any sun blocking properties AT ALL. So that's false advertising right there. They aren't for use in the sun. They don't darken anything.
As far as audio quality... they are a cool concept, but again, falls short of expectations. The open ear design means the speakers have to work harder to be audible. That means they often make those tin-sounding rattles that tiny speakers make when cranked up too high. This is definitely NOT cool for music as most of the fidelity is lost right off the bat, and adding insult to injury is that they often don't get loud enough to use outside. I'm not saying using it in a crowded subway terminal (that you can just forget about completely), I'm talking about even just going for a stroll around my suburban block with some birds chirping and the wind blowing lightly, maybe a car driving in the distance. I tried listening to a recorded lecture (since music was a lost cause), and they couldn't get loud enough to hear clearly. The microphone for calls was OK in my test, so I guess they are cool as a way to take a phone call without wearing a headset, but that only works if you're wearing these anyway as sunglasses. They aren't sunglasses, so you wouldn't be wearing them anyway, and you wouldn't be wearing them for music, and you wouldn't be wearing them to make a phone call either because they rarely get loud enough unless you are home alone... in which case you can put your phone on speaker and avoid this whole mess.
In conclusion- its a good idea but executed poorly and does NOT live up to expectations. I'm surprised there are so many good reviews on this product. I can't think of a time I would use it.
text_fidelity_b: OhO Audio Sunglasses,Open Ear Audio Sunglasses Speaker to Listen Music and Make Phone Calls,Water Resistance and Full UV Lens Protection for Outdoor Sports and Compatiable for All Smart Phones

HP Stream 7 32GB Windows 8.1 Tablet (Includes Office 365 Personal for One Year) I was really looking forward to trying this tablet out. To date I'd had no exposure to Windows 8.1 or a dedicated Windows tablet. I have had a decent 10.1 inch Android tablet.

First are foremost, the elephant in the room... or rather, the mouse. This is a seven inch wide screen tablet. I have friends whose who online lives are conducted via five inch cell phone screens and they're happy with it. The screen on this tablet is nice. Don't get me wrong. I was able to stream from Amazon video in HD (720) and the video was crisp and clean. Images display well but, again, the screen is just seven inches. I can't imagine trying to be productive with something so small.

For a device with only one gig of RAM this runs Windows fairly well. I wws able to load several Windows programs including the Calibrě eBook manager which took a little longer to convert eBooks between formats but did the job. I also loaded a legacy email and Usenet program that I've been using for a decade or longer. Along with directly installed programs I also downloaded a handful of apps from the very buggy Microsoft app store. The store worked less than 50% of the time while I was trying this tablet out. I at one point had to resort to switching to a local login account and then back to my Hotmail logi. It only took about an hour of reading web forums to find that solution to the Windows app store refusing to work.

Two problems I ran into were the sound which is from a single speaker hidden in a slot on one of the short sides of the tablet. If you want to listen to anything other than the default Window's beeps and tones you'll want to pair this with a blue tooth speaker or headphones. The speaker in this tablet is deplorable. The next problem I had was the tablet runs HOT. I was running a program designed for Windows 98, downloading and reading posts un Usenet and viewing a few posted vacation and astronomy images and I had to stop. The tablet was so hot it was uncomfortable to hold and I worried it might overheat and become damaged.

While I was impressed to see Windows running on a small tablet I was thoroughly unimpressed with Windows 8.1 the tile system is just terrible.

So, it has good video quality on a too small screen with horrible sound and a flaky app store to rely upon, though you can download and install normal Windows programs. I just wasn't that crazy about this tablet. And will definitely be sticking with Android and a much larger screen.
text_fidelity_b: HP Stream 7 32GB Windows 8.1 Tablet (Includes Office 365 Personal for One Year)

Sent it to Canon for repair. Got an email saying they didn't work on that part, I'd get a new or refurbished. I called to say i did not want a refurbished camera given that i'd already had problems with two of this model.  Too bad they said, you're getting refurbished.  I asked to talk to customer relations. Got a lady who told me it was in the warranty they could give me refurbished and furthermore they had no new ones to give--this is the CAnon facility mind you. Back to initial rep who refused to let me talk to anyone else and refused to budge on sending a new camera, even though it was an option in the email. I wrote letters and emails to management. Got a response, said they'd send me a new camera after i said i had the whole thing on recording and was thinking of posting to youtube. but they wouldn't pay for me to ship the old one back.  Anyway this story goes on and on, including me mailing the camera back and being told it actually WAS a new one and they were shipping the same camera back to me.  Was a nightmare. I don't know if any of the other companies are better, but i've been a solid Canon customer for 20 years--as i told them--and I won't be anymore.  They need to take lessons from Amazon on customer service.  Hope this camera lasts awhile as I know now it won't get serviced properly without it being more trouble than it's worth.

Buffalo Anti-Glare Screen Protector Kit for Kindle Fire HDX 7" (will only fit Kindle Fire HDX 7"), 2 pack I tried the Anti Glare screen protector rather than the clear so I could use my Fire out at the barn and dressage arena in the sunlight more easily. It was super easy to install and took less than two minutes. I cleaned my screen with a lens wipe first to ensure it was free of lint, finger prints and oils. Followed the included instructions exactly and lined up the screen protector with the Fire's camera etc and laid it down. The package had a stiff cardboard piece that works better than a credit card to smooth the protector sheet as you go - I have no air bubbles at all on the first try. text_fidelity_a:
Logitech G502 Proteus Spectrum RGB Tunable Gaming Mouse, 12,000 DPI On-The-Fly DPI Shifting, Personalized Weight and Balance Tuning with (5) 3.6g Weights, 11 Programmable Buttons I’m not a hardcore gamer anymore, so for the past few years, I’ve been using a Logitech M570 Wireless Trackball (thumb trackball). I like trackballs for everyday use, and it’s adequate for casual World of Warcraft playing. Most of the time I just futz around leveling alts or doing 5 mans with friends.

But lately I’ve been wanting a mouse I can customize, with more options to adjust my playstyle. It’s cold in my house in the winter, so I wanted to set up mouseover macros and use more mouse buttons, because my hands are cold sitting on the keyboard. So the G502 Proteus Spectrum seemed like a good mouse to review.

I just had one problem: my computer can’t customize the mouse. Why? I have a Mac Book Air.

Now, I know the G502 says on the box that it supports Windows. There’s no mention of Mac support. But I’ve never had a problem with my Mac recognizing Logitech mice, so I figured I’d be safe. What I didn’t know is that Logitech gaming mice have separate software from the Logitech Control Center for regular Logitech mice.

After some Googling, I found the Logitech Gaming Software, which supports Mac OS X 10.8.x and up. I installed it on a Mavericks machine and a Yosemite machine. Neither computer’s Logitech Gaming Software was able to find the mouse. The G502 Proteus CORE is supported, but not the G502 Proteus SPECTRUM.

So right now, I’m unable to customize any of the extra buttons or RGB lighting or any of the other special features. It’s a really fancy basic mouse. I will continue to check for Proteus Spectrum support in the Mac Logitech Gaming Center, and update this review when I can customize things. I’m going into so much detail on the Mac side of things because I know I’m not the only Mac person who tried to use this mouse. I think there’s a workaround with Bootcamp or using a Windows computer, but I’m unable to try that.

I did use the mouse for a few weeks, to test the comfort. I’m really picky on how mice feel in my hand. I’m female and have smaller hands. I like how this mouse didn’t feel too short, and it wasn’t too heavy or wide for me to use comfortably for hours at a time. I also liked the included weights, so you can adjust the weight of the mouse. I haven’t had a mouse with an adjustable weight before, and I liked that extra level of customization.
text_fidelity_b: Logitech G502 Proteus Spectrum RGB Tunable Gaming Mouse, 12,000 DPI On-The-Fly DPI Shifting, Personalized Weight and Balance Tuning with (5) 3.6g Weights, 11 Programmable Buttons

JAM XT Extreme Wireless Speaker, Splash Proof, Drop Proof, Dirt Proof IP64 Rating, Carabiner Clip, Built-in Speakerphone, Works with iPhone, Android, Bluetooth Devices, HXP430BK Black I must say this little guy is impressive. For it's size it rocked out in my back porch. Due to the IP64 rating it's a bit heavy but that's a good thing.

I tested this speaker paired with a Sony android phone. Bluetooth pairing was instant. While I didn't quite get a full 30 foot range, I found the actual 27 foot range to be acceptable.

I dropped the speaker from my waist height of 36" onto the concrete pad on my porch. No issues with playability or broken pieces. Although I did notice a slight scuff mark. No biggie.

I like the carabiner feature for hanging the speaker, from a tent ceiling, tree, or post. But I don't see anyone hanging the speaker off a backpack. The weight will cause it to swing wildly. In fact it's heavy enough to be stored in the bottom of your pack.

Recharging was easy, but the rubber plug takes a little finesse to put it back into place.

The sound was crisp with somewhat deep bass undertones. I didn't expect this little speaker to pump out heavy bass, but it's adequate for its size.

I don't recommend that you crank this up too loud when camping in the woods. The loud music might drown out the sounds of an attacking bear or wildebeest.

For the money it's a decent wireless speaker that will survive most outdoor adventures.

text_fidelity_a:
VANGUARD GH-200 Tripod Heads This is my 2nd GH-200 tripod head. The first one I received through the Vine program was defective and was returned to Vanguard and exchanged. The replacement I received operates much better than the first.

I tested this tripod head with my [[ASIN:B001D60LG8 Dolica AX620B100 62-Inch Proline Tripod]] and my Kodak Z990 camera.

At full tension release there is just enough friction to give some confident feedback of movement. It allows responsive and fairly easy tracking of moving objects. The tension knob has approximately ¼ turn of adjustment giving some range of friction preferences. At full lock I found the head to be rock solid with no play or give. The pistol grip has a release handle that allows you to set the tension knob to full lock but have the ability to squeeze the grip and quickly reposition the camera. The spring in the grip is not adjustable and is insanely stiff. After a half hour of testing out this tripod head my hand was aching from the force necessary to squeeze the grip release. In their product description they claim you can track an object "ultra smoothly by pressing the trigger" I did not find this to be the case. You can reposition the camera by squeezing the trigger but at full lock the grip release did not give smooth movement or ease of tracking.

The pistol grip has a quick, one hand operation, release collar that allows the grip to be rotated 360 degrees with eight locking points. This collar and release are affected by the friction setting for the ball head.

I'm not a fan of their mounting system. First because the screw to attach the plate to the camera does not have a butterfly handle. A coin or screwdriver is required to mount or dismount the plate from or to the camera. Second, while partially released the plate can be adjusted forward or back to get better balance of your rig. There is a pin on the head keeping the plate and camera from falling forward or backward off the mount. Unfortunately there is no positive safety lock. Just a few turns on the tension knob for the camera plate and your camera is completely free of the head.

The mounting plate itself can be unlocked to turn 360 degree panoramic shots. There are 72 click points that are 5 degrees of rotation apart. Even with my relatively light Kodak Z990 on this head the clicks became indistinct and hard to notice. Still, it's a nice feature to capture smooth panoramic shots.

The tripod mount is threaded for 1/4" or, with an easily removed adapter sleeve, 3/8" screw. This tripod head did not come with the small tool to remove the adapter sleeve that other Vanguard products do but as with the camera plate a screwdriver or coin will do the job.

In the end I can't say I'm a complete fan of this tripod head. Itappears to be quite sturdy and should give years of service. Unfortunately, for me, the lack of secure locking of the camera plate and the extreme pressure needed to squeeze the trigger release we enough negatives to make this less than stellar. I can't say that I was wow'd by it.
text_fidelity_b: VANGUARD GH-200 Tripod Heads

text_fidelity_a:
adidas RPT-01 Bluetooth Sport On-Ear Headphones - Night Grey, 2.8 x 5.6 x 7.5 Inches I wear headphones when I work outside, spring through fall. By the end of fall, that year’s pair is pretty nasty from hours of daily use and me sweating in them. Of course I clean them, but it’s impossible to *really* deep clean headphones.

So that’s what drew me to the adidas RPT-01 Sport Headphones: the description advertises “removable, washable knitted ear cushions.” Knit covers I can wash? Hooray!

But there’s no instructions in the box on how to remove the ear covers or the headband. It turns out the cushions aren’t as removable as advertised.The ear cups twist off the headphones (a gentle, counter-clockwise turn), but there’s still an inner plastic rim. I thought I’d be able to wash the knitted cover itself, but nope. And I nearly tore the cover trying to figure out how to remove it, until I found the manual online.

I can’t figure out how to get the headband all the way off. The black plastic lining is removable, allowing the headband to be pushed up. I worry the headband will tear quickly, as the holes that line up with the black plastic lining aren’t reinforced.

Sound quality is okay … as long as I don’t use the Control Knob.

The Control Knob is like a volume rocker and skip/go back button in one. But when I used it to change the volume and skip tracks, I had static that lasted for several seconds.

There is an adidas Headphones app, but I thought it was useless. The only advantage of the app is that it allows you to set up to 3 customizable actions for the other button on the headphones. Oddly enough, at the time of writing this review, the app was only available on Android. I wanted to test the headphones on an iPhone too, but could not because the adidas Headphones app wasn’t available in my country (USA).

Lastly, the headphones are so uncomfortable to wear that I can’t wear them for more than 10 minutes. If I were inclined to use them, which I’m not, mainly because of the static whenever I use the Control Knob. I have a small head, but these headphones are tight and squeeze my ears and head. The ear cushions are actually quite scratchy too.
text_fidelity_b: adidas RPT-01 Bluetooth Sport On-Ear Headphones - Night Grey, 2.8 x 5.6 x 7.5 Inches

Aoybevty USB C to USB C 3.1/3.2 Cable 6FT, 10Gbps Data Transfer 100W Fast Charging 4K@60Hz Video Monitor Cable for Thunderbolt 4/3 Laptop Tablet Cell Phone USB Type C Electronics Devices This usb type-c to type-c cable is costs a little more than other cables you may see because it is not just a charging cable.

When it comes to the Type-C port, consumers now need to have a phd in electronics just to understand what works with what. There are just so many standards crammed into this reversible port that you need to really read the fine print to know whether it will work for your uses. What's worse is that once you throw these cables into a drawer, good luck finding the right one.

Type-C cables that come with your phone or phone charger will generally only be good for charging your phone, but not great for transferring data. This Type-C cable will carry up to 100w of power, meaning it will charge your phone or tablet at the highest speed it can support. When transferring data, this cable will allow you to copy files at the highest USB 3.1 speeds.

But more than that, this cable supports video signals so that it will be usable to connect your laptop or phone to a portable type-c monitor (assuming your devices support it).

Personally, I got this cable to work with a pair of NReal Air video glasses so that I have a backup to the cable included in the box. These cables work but are a little bit stiff.
text_fidelity_b: Aoybevty USB C to USB C 3.1/3.2 Cable 6FT, 10Gbps Data Transfer 100W Fast Charging 4K@60Hz Video Monitor Cable for Thunderbolt 4/3 Laptop Tablet Cell Phone USB Type C Electronics Devices

Patriot LX Series 64GB High Speed Micro SDXC Class 10 UHS-I Transfer Speeds For Action Cameras, Phones, Tablets, and PCs So I bought this to use with my 128GB Lenovo Yoga as a secondary drive. When I plugged it into my computer to transfer some files, it shows 116GBs - what it should be for a 128GB drive. Though I really wish computers and manufacturers would calculate memory the same, that is another matter.

I went to transfer a folder with 61 GBs of memory. It got about 3/4 done and it decided it was full. With about 50GBs, my 116 GB card is FULL. It should be only about half full. This is a problem. I am not happy about this and will not buy another one of these. I will format it and try again. Maybe there are hidden files that aren't showing up on it. But this is really annoying.

Update: I decided to format the drive and found that the bit size for exFAT is very small. As in less than my file size small. I changed it to NTSF, as it will only be used in a computer, and it is now working properly as regards to being able to actually fill it with 116 GBs. But it still took about 4 hours to copy 8 GBs of data to it. My USB 3.0 drive would have done it in less than 30 minutes.
text_fidelity_b: Patriot LX Series 64GB High Speed Micro SDXC Class 10 UHS-I Transfer Speeds For Action Cameras, Phones, Tablets, and PCs

TomTom Via 1525SE 5 Inch GPS Navigation Device with Free Traffic, Free Maps of the US, Advanced Lane Guidance and Spoken Turn-By-Turn Directions This GPS is a real upgrade for me, but I still love my old one which is TomTom One. Too bad it's no longer supported by TomTom or I probably would not have chosen the TomTom Via 1525 to try out for review. The very first thing I noticed about it was that the screen was twice as large as on my One - a very coveted perk to me. I choose to still use separate GPS devices instead of my phone since my phone uses up data and the GPS doesn't, saving me $$.

I have only used the Via 1525 a couple of times and it worked perfectly. I had to make a new account to TomTom to update it and overall it took about an hour and a half. I had a couple of problems with the update and had to restart but it finally worked. It comes with a USB for charging from a computer and another to use in the auxiliary power port in the car, and a mounting disk to adhere to a good spot in the car. It's not as intuitive as I would like, but it's not hard to figure out and it took us straight to our destination both times. I purposely passed some streets it was telling to me turn on to just to see how fast it would recalculate a route and it recalculated quickly. It has a lot of options that are indicated on the product page, most of which I will probably not use.

It's too early yet to give it 5 stars, but definitely 4 for now. It's a GPS, it found satellites quickly, got me a route planned out and was easy to follow. What more do I want from it? I like it a lot. It's supposed to have lifetime traffic and lifetime maps.......or until TomTom stops supporting it too.

text_fidelity_a:
Logitech C922x Pro + Logitech for Creators Litra Glow - The Ultimate Solution for a Professional Look During Video-Calls I am comparing this to a Logitech C910 HD 1080p webcam which I've been using almost daily since 2012.

I don't stream games but I stream my live DJ broadcasts. I use 4 webcams and a green screen. I use xSplit exclusively.

This C922x Pro Stream is for gamers so they can stream on Twitch or YouTube. The camera is supposed to automatically load a background removing program so you don't have to use a green screen. This special software, Personify ChromaCam, is free when have the C922. Installing is another matter entirely. Myself, like others, have older, but capable systems that cannot install this software. I checked on Personify's website and the PC requirements are: Processor: Intel 4th generation or higher Core CPU, or the AMD equivalent (Quad core AMD Phenom), OS: Windows 7, 8, 10, and Memory: 4GB+ RAM. My system, even though its 3 years old, meets all these specs but when installing I get a 'unable to install due to ABX or ADX" something.

The camera's clarity is not any better than my 4 year old C910. In fact, my C910 has Carl Zeiss, the new cam doesn't not. The colors appear washed out with too much brightness. I expected better, but the C922 regressed a bit in the lens department.

Now here's a kicker for you...you cannot, and I mean, cannot, view the camera while changing it's settings. Yes, you heard me right. Open the camera settings and you get a windowed box for changing the settings, but the webcam does not come on or is it viewable. So, am I supposed to change the settings, open the cam, close the cam, change the settings, open the cam...etc..etc?

The mount is sturdy and multi-positional. I like the added tripod adapter. At this price point there should be a privacy shield.

I had an issue getting the camera to initially turn on. The outer ring would flash but no camera picture. Then I realized that some webcams don't like being plugged into a USB hub. After adding an extension cord and plugging in directly to my PC the cam worked.

The big question...is this camera worth the $50 more than the entry level C920 series camera? For the money you get a ChromaCam program which may or may not work and you get 6 months free xSplit service. Hmmmmm...OBS, which is quite capable, is a free service.

Logitech has so many choices lately, each with increased pricing. Let's face it, it's all about the price. Do you really need your ugly mug put up in a live game? Probably not since it's going to use PC resources that would be better used for gaming. For the $50 extra you could get a couple decent games, or a new mouse, or a mouse pad, or a boat load of peanuts.

The choice is yours.
text_fidelity_b: Logitech C922x Pro + Logitech for Creators Litra Glow - The Ultimate Solution for a Professional Look During Video-Calls

Final E3000 in-Ear Headphones, Hi-Fi Sound Quality, Hires Certified, Award Winning, Stainless Steel Housing, 3.5mm Standard Plug, Natural Sound with Extended Bass, Designed in Japan I am not shy about returning headphones I don't like but these are KEEPERS. This might be the happiest I've been with some earphones since my beloved Nuforce NE-700X. But to be fair those cost $90 in 2014.

Update after 2 weeks of use:

I went to a larger tip and now they don't sit as far in my ear. The bass and soundstage both improved with more air around the instruments. I really like these. I don't find myself thinking oh they do this, or they don't do that with regard to sound. The just play the music. That little TINY bit of graininess is gone with some break in I guess. While I don't listen to Metal or EDM they handle all genres of music well and handle more complex music like rock well compared to others I have tried. They come with 4 size tips so finding the right size is easier compared to pairs that only come with 3 size tips. The tips grip the nozzle really well but still come off and go on pretty easily. They come with some really small ear hooks but I haven't tried them yet. There is no listening fatigue yet they are still pretty accurate. They do not go really loud but they do go loud enough for me.I haven't played with EQ much because I haven't felt the need. Wires are thin and tangle pretty easily and don't untangle very easily. I have not noticed any microphonics. Of course, I'd like to have $100 buds but for $55 dollars they hit my nice but I won't cry if I lose them price point.

===========================================
Original review

They are not even broken in yet (and they don't need it) but my only real complaint and it's nitpicky, but they have a touch of graininess. But nowhere near as much as the Carbo Tenor. These are very neutra with decent detail while never being too bright. There is nice seperation between instruments but not much of a soundstage but there is nice amount of 'air' around the intruments. They do not have a lot of extension but they are not bass shy like the Carbo Tenor were. Drums sound natural, again not like the Carbo Tenor where they sounded more like carboard boxes.

They are very light so they very comfortable. (I like straight earphones the best) The default tips fit me the best which is a nice change for me. There is next to no strain relief on the earphones as you can see in the picture so if you are hard on headphones, maybe consider other phones. on the good side the lack of strain relief makes them very comfortable worn wire up which i want for the gym. They have vents on the back so I doubt that isolation is very good for in-ear phones.

In summary these are nuetral sounding with out any of the 'problems' of hifi. They are never over sibilant and they do not punish badly recorded songs or when listening to low bit rate stuff like pandora. I would call them fun for working out but they are not too dry if the quality of the music is what you want. They are not going to impress anyone or give you an eargasm when listening to your best music. But at $54 I'm extemely please with them and for me are a big step up from the Carbo Tenor unless you are impressed by a forward/blaring sound.
text_fidelity_b: Final E3000 in-Ear Headphones, Hi-Fi Sound Quality, Hires Certified, Award Winning, Stainless Steel Housing, 3.5mm Standard Plug, Natural Sound with Extended Bass, Designed in Japan

The outside material feels like a cross between linen and leather...soft without being slippery and it doesn't catch dust or fingerprints on the front. Belkin USB 2.0 4-Port Ultra-Mini Hub My mother contacted me because she needed a USB hub. I don't recall how she found out about them, but off I went to research what she needed. I first questioned her on her requirements, then researched the status of USB standards (now version 3.0 is out compared to the last time I needed to look), and then did my market research. I reduced it down to 3 hubs and this one won hands down due to it's compactness, support of old and new USB standard versions, and it looked like it was going to be easy for her to set it up on her own. My Mom, btw, is 75+ years old.

The report back from her was that it was exactly what she needed. She hooked everything up and it all just started working. No fuss at all, she said. I've got to give her a lot of credit for being pretty good with the computer.

The fact that I didn't have to troubleshoot it from 250+ miles away means I give it 5 stars too!

I bought it for her 3 months ago now and she hasn't had any troubles and I hope it stays that way. Belkin's products are reputable for quality and in this case a little ingenuity. Highly recommended!

text_fidelity_a: OREI 4x4 HDMI 4K 2.0V Matrix Switch/splitter, (4-Input, 4-Output) with Remote Control Supports Full UltraHD 1080P, 4K X 2K It seems to work fine for everything but games, and it seems that the sound processor may be the source of the audio and video glitches. Certain sounds seem to cause more problems than others, including dropped audio, glitchy video, and sometimes a blank screen. This happens with both XBox Ones and a PS3. I mainly play Forza 6 and Gran Turismo 6, and certain engine sounds seem to be associated with these problems more than others. Streaming video doesn't seem to cause any problems with any of the input devices or either TV. The normal solution is to cycle the power off and back on. Different cables or settings don't seem to make a difference. I'm not using the audio splitter at all. Personal opinion (from decades of experience with processors of all kinds), is that whatever processor is used simply cannot process some sounds correctly, even to pass the signal through. I may be wrong. I've been wrong before. This may be a quality control issue, or it may be an engineering issue. Either way, I'm looking for a better product, and most of the ones in this price range seem to be identical except for the name on the box. In fact, many more expensive devices seem to be exactly the same layout, and likely use the same circuitry. There's no way to tell from the name on the box, or the Amazon description.
text_fidelity_b: OREI 4x4 HDMI 4K 2.0V Matrix Switch/splitter, (4-Input, 4-Output) with Remote Control Supports Full UltraHD 1080P, 4K X 2K

text_fidelity_a:
Sony RX100 IV 20.1 MP Premium Compact Digital Camera w/ 1-inch Sensor, 4K Movies and 40x Super Slow Motion HD DSCRX100M4/B Black For the simple fact that this camera can do EVERYTHING I want it to do in my pocket, it get 5+ stars. I could go on for days about this camera, but I will try to hold this review to my personal game-changers.

HFR: Shooting video at 1080p, 120fps (100MB) and slowing down the footage in post produces better slow-mo videos compared to the HFR feature that can do 1080p 240fps at the best quality. The ultra HFR feature was a big sell for me, but I feel like 480fps and 960fps have garbage quality and it's really really difficult to get the timing right when you are taking the shot in that feature mode because you only have a 2 second timeframe. I must have spent 2 hours trying to get a slow-mo shot of a bee in my garden when I first bought it, but could never get the timing right on pressing record when the stupid bee would start flying. Shooting in normal video mode at 120fps and slowing down in post at 24fps is seriously amazing, and I will likely never use the HFR again.

Time-Lapse: Pay the $9.99 extra to download this app, because holy cow, it is freaking awesome. There is full manual control over intervals, # shots, etc, and it blows me away that it can produce day-night time-lapse with little to no flicker and amazing color with accurate white balance throughout. If you don't want the hassle of editing the stills in post, then you can just have the camera produce a 1080p 24fps video file in-camera, although post allows you more creativity and ability to produce 4k time lapse.
Slog2: I've been shooting all my videos in Slog2 (4k & 1080p) since I bought the camera several months ago, and up until just now I did not have a computer beefy enough to process the footage in post (which is the reason I have waited on posting my review). For the last week, I've been color grading my Slog2 footage with the Color Finale plugin in Final Cut Pro X. The footage is stunning and the dynamic range blows me away. I'm still trying to figure out the over exposure sweet spot of shooting in Slog2, but for the most part it looks really nice when shot at +1 - +2 stops over exposed and re-adjusted in post. There's not as much noise in the shadows as I expected, and I'm about to get the Neat Video Noise Reduction plugin that I expect to help with the little noise that I'm seeing. I went out to Joshua Tree for the meteor shower and shot 4k 24fps video of the stars, which is insane for a little camera like this.

Lens: Having the faster lens fully zoomed in (f2.8) compared to the RX100 M1's f4.9 is changed the way I take photos of my baby. It really was difficult to get a decent bokeh shooting at typical portrait focal lengths with the M1, but very easy now with the M4. Fast, clean and crisp, this lens is great.

Compact Size: I wanted a camera that I can put in my pocket. As long as you don't wear skinny jeans, then you're good to go. I don't wear skinny jeans, but I'm just saying. Cargos are the best, but then I realize that I've become the dad that wears cargos, and then I see the guy in Honduras swapping heavy lenses with a dslr around his neck and don't feel so bad. Although, I often worry when it's in my pocket that the lens ring control might bend and not be as smooth as it is, but that hasn't happened.

Focus Modes: Changing between focus modes is my one gripe about this camera. In a run and gun environment, I have not been able to figure out how to easily toggle between the various auto focus modes. It's easy to go between MF and AF, but trying to toggle between the AF modes when trying to get the right video clip of my active baby is extremely difficult. However, note that using the lens ring in AF mode for rack focusing is possible, which I wasn't able to do on the RX100 M1.

Overall, I wanted a camera that could do EVERYTHING, do everything WELL, and that EVERYTHING it does WELL could fit in my pocket….
text_fidelity_b: Sony RX100 IV 20.1 MP Premium Compact Digital Camera w/ 1-inch Sensor, 4K Movies and 40x Super Slow Motion HD DSCRX100M4/B Black

Pioneer Active in-Ear Wireless Headphones with Integrated Clip, Red SE-CL5BT(R) At the price (about $40 on Amazon), I expected more from these PIONEER ACTIVE IN-EAR WIRELESS HEADPHONES WITH INTEGRATED CLIP (Red SE-CL5BT(R)). The sound is very clear, which is obviously the most important thing. However, I find the controls (3 tiny, flat buttons) to be fumbly and difficult to use. The fact that the buttons have dual functions (e.g., one button increases the volume when pressed once, and advances music to the next track when pressed and held) is partly to blame. However, the buttons seem slow to respond, so I am constantly pressing and holding when all I want is the press once function.

The headphones paired with both my iPad Pro and my Galaxy S7 smartphone, but NOT particularly easily. To place the headphones in pairing mode, so that your Bluetooth device can see the Pioneer broadcast in the device Settings, you must press and hold the headphones’ center button until a miniscule LED light on the side of the clip blinks alternately red and blue. (Normally, the light is red when the headphones are charging, and slowly-blinking blue when the headphones are turned on and connected.)

What’s hard about that pairing, you may ask? It’s in the instructions, except that the instructions are printed in type so tiny that even the best eyes will need a magnifying glass to read them. Worse yet, the key instructions are printed in pale gray (like grayed-out PC menu selections) on soft, recycled paper that is also gray. Purchasers deserve instructions that are printed in black ink, at the very least.

The clip is nice to have. The battery life isn’t great (about 8 hours), and the battery takes about 2 hours to charge via the included USB cable. The “carrying case” for the extra ear tips (you get size S, M, and L sets) is a small resealable plastic bag. The headphones don’t have “over ear” fit (as stated at least once on the product page), but are strictly “in ear” fit (i.e., battery-powered earbuds).

I didn't try using these earphones to answer telephone calls. However, considering how many mistakes I make with the tiny buttons when playing music, I suspect that I'd be hanging up a lot when I was trying to take calls.

text_fidelity_a:
DeLorme Earthmate PN-40 Waterproof Hiking GPS I purchased a Delorme PN-40 GPS for the purpose of geocaching. I already own a Garmin GPSMap 60CSx and a Garmin eTrex Legend, so although I did not really need another unit I wanted one so that when geocaching with my kids we would each be carrying a GPS and not reliant on one another. I have been very satisfied with my Garmin units but was impressed with the reviews and feature set of the Delorme, so I bought it with the expectation of it being acceptable for my uses as a backup unit. It has exceeded my expectations. It is not without flaws but it is a tremendous GPS that is very much worth every penny of the purchase price.

It is very similar in hard interface layout to my 60CSx, with the same buttons doing similar functions though in different locations. This makes working with the Delorme simple in that I immediately found myself familiar with how to work this GPS. The software interface is different, though, and is unlike any other unit with which I have worked. Different is not wrong, but it means a learning curve for those who use Garmin or Magellan units.

The first power-on of this unit is the most painful as it searches for the satellites. After this initial acquisition, however, power-up is always appreciably faster and the acquisition of satellites faster.

Once the GPS has acquired the satellites, it has proven itself to be very accurate and stable. It is not unusual to navigate to a location and have the unit lead me to a point less than a foot away from the lat/long specified. Reported accuracy on the screen is typically between 6 and 11 feet.

The accuracy does diminish under heavy canopy but no more so than my Garmins do. In dense tree cover I found that it maintains its location quite well most of the time, though it occasionally gets confused and leads me in circles. It seems to do this at times when my 60CSx is having no trouble, but it also seems to have no trouble when the Garmins are confused. This brings up a good point - different GPS manufacturers, using differing chip sets, will have varying environments in which their GPS units work better than others and sometimes not as well as others. It is important to keep this in mind and to select a unit that is best suited for the need.

The compass is excellent. Once calibrated it seems to be very accurate and does not need for the unit to be held level flat when in use in order to get a correct bearing. The 3D compass is something that is lacking in my Garmin units, but newer units have this feature now and it's wonderful. Manually calibrating the compass is easy and all you have to do is to follow the instructions on the screen (it equates to a series of arm motions).

This is a rugged and sturdy unit and can handle some jostling. It does as well in wet, rainy weather as it does on clear days. It is waterproof and can be submerged, but I am not daring enough to try this voluntarily.

One point on which many people complain is the screen size. Yes, it has a smaller screen than average units but it also seems to be bright and readable even in direct sunlight. Sure, larger would be nice but clear and readable is far preferable.

Delorme ships their Topo product with this GPS and it is the deal-maker that gives this GPS a decided edge. The maps may be cut and transferred to the PN-40 through Topo, or the pre-cut maps may be used instead. To get Garmin's MapSource costs an extra $100, which makes the PN-40 an even better deal. The maps are of good quality and are sufficient for hiking and driving alike. For most uses the pre-cup maps will be sufficient, but higher resolution images can be cut from Topo.

Right out of the box, my PN-40 was defective and had problem with the screen. I was not convinced that it was a problem until I called Delorme, and I was told to ship it back. In one week's time I had a completely new unit that has worked flawlessly ever since. While I was disappointed with the first unit being defective, I was shocked at how responsive Delorme is to customer requests for assistance. It is clear to me that they stand behind their product.

Less than three weeks after I purchased my PN-40, Delorme released Topo 8. My unit shipped with Topo 7. I called Delorme and asked about an upgrade, and for the cost of shipping a new Topo 8 DVD set was sent to me.

Map updates on the PN-40 are FAST. Scrolling is not exactly smooth but the dual-core processor embedded within keeps up quite admirably.

One drawback with this unit is that, at this time, importing waypoints and geocaches requires a different software set than can be used with Garmin and Magellan units. It can be done with Topo, and for geocachers there is Cache Register, but GSAK and other common tools do not transfer successfully at this time. Hopefully this will be remedied in the near future. Granted, this is easy enough to do, but one cannot have a single software application that can work with multiple units of different brand.

Another drawback is that this GPS loves batteries. On new, fully-charged NiMH batteries one can expect maybe 10 hours of operation before the unit gracefully turns itself off. On a long trek it is therefore a good idea to bring along extra batteries. Because alkalines tend to drain more quickly in electronics, I would recommend using either NiMH or lithium batteries.

The Delorme PN-40 is a very nice GPS for consumer use. It is accurate, it holds its signal well, has a great display and comes with Topo which combined all make this unit hard to pass up. It's not perfect by any means, but it is still excellent and should be considered when looking for a good handheld GPS.
text_fidelity_b: DeLorme Earthmate PN-40 Waterproof Hiking GPS

This one has a USB-C port, unlike one of my others, but - unlike the one I have that does have USB-C - the total current is more limited. Both adapters with USB-C ports only support 5v output, so they may not charge your device if your device can only accept higher voltage (USB-C has multiple layers of standards, so can be a bit confusing).

I like this adapter when traveling to multiple regions within one trip. Otherwise, I'll just use the cheap adapters which by themselves are smaller. Out of the three I own, I'm not sure which is best; I think it depends on your personal situation. Hopefully I shared enough to help you decide.

Monoprice Blackbird 4K 3x1 HDMI 1.4 Switch - Compact, HDCP 2.2, Built-in Equalizer, 4K 30Hz, YCbCr 4:4:4, 18Gbps (Compatible with PS4/5 Xbox Apple TV Fire Stick Roku Blu-Ray Player) Since we mounted our TV we like to use as few chords as possible. This way they are neatly tucked along the wall and down into the entertainment center where all our entertainment equipment is housed. So the main HDMI cable runs down but of course we have more components that require a cable than the one connected to the TV. Our solution? A signal splitter. Thankfully, we have only three output connections so this one seemed perfect. Plus, it touts 4k signal, even though most pre-4k HDMI boxes should be fine, but it's nice to have that in the title just in case.

What I use this mostly for is the cable box and a couple of video game systems. As for the cable box, seems to work fine; no dropped signals that I've noticed, nor any degradation in quality. As for game consoles, I have the PS3 and the Wii U hooked up to it. SAme: no noticeable quality degradation nor input lag.
Now, to put it to the real test, I hooked up some retro consoles that have been modded to output native HDMI; that means they'll be HDMI with no lag. Considering I have this and two HDMI cables connecting the console to the TV, I was curious to see if there truly was any lag.
With older games, timing is everything, especially on the 8-bit consoles with platformers and fighters, like the NES. From what I could tell, there was absolutely no lag, not to mention signal loss. The buttons responded as though I were using a normal NES on a CRT.

So yeah, I'm pretty satisfied. It's a bit light and doesn't have heavy pads on the bottom to prevent it from sliding around. With so many cables, and the ability to use the remote control, it should be a bit more stable on the surface.
I haven't used the remote as the detections are instant. No need to manually switch the inputs, at least from my experience. Also, I didn't need to use the power adapter; the power from the HDMI cables seemed to be sufficient, and the detection was not complicated by the lack of adapter. Weird.
text_fidelity_b: Monoprice Blackbird 4K 3x1 HDMI 1.4 Switch - Compact, HDCP 2.2, Built-in Equalizer, 4K 30Hz, YCbCr 4:4:4, 18Gbps (Compatible with PS4/5 Xbox Apple TV Fire Stick Roku Blu-Ray Player)

Tiffen 82VND 82 Millimeter Variable ND Filter Shooting video outdoors with a DSLR requires, obviously, proper exposure. When shooting at 24 (23.978) frames per second, the normal shutter speed should be 1/50th of a second (1/60 at 29.97 fps). If the camera is set at the lowest ISO rating of 100, in bright daylight the f/stop would be around f/22. If you want to operate at wider aperture to achieve shallow depth of field, you need to cut the light.

This variable density filter allows such an adjustment. The problem is that it cuts the light by rotating two polarizing filters against each other. Polarizers can be tricky and, by design, modify the quality of light. Thus it may act unexpectedly.

One downside is that the front of the filter is not threaded and my 77mm model is a larger diameter than the 70-200mm Nikon zoom it fits on. So now the bayonet lens hood won't fit. Now I'm outdoors with a filter on the lens and no hood to block flare. There aren't any hoods that naturally fit the filter so you need to tape a hood to the outer ring or use a matte box.
text_fidelity_b: Tiffen 82VND 82 Millimeter Variable ND Filter
