Netgear R7500-200NAS Nighthawk X4 Ultimate Gaming Router - AC2350 4X4 MU-MIMO Dual Band WiFi Gigabit Router (R7500v2) with Open Source Support. Compatible with Amazon Echo/Alexa I'm not a gamer, but I do have around 30 devices connected to a home network. These include WEMO switches, Amazon Echos, a smart TV, a playstation, Kindles, iPads, printers, and smartphones. The "dynamic Quality of Service" feature of this NIGHTHAWK X4 ULTIMATE GAMING ROUTER (R7500v2) seems to prioritize these devices, so that all of them are more responsive (faster connections) than they were with my previous router (a rock-solid NIGHTHAWK (R7000)).

When this NIGHTHAWK (R7500v2) is set up, it recognizes all of the "Internet of things" devices for what they are. In the "attached devices" list, these aren't given device names (e.g., "iPad", picked up from the device itself) but have "n/a" in the name column (and you can't assign them names even if you know them by the MAC numbers). I don't know exactly how the "Quality of Service" feature performs its magic, but now when I ask an Amazon Echo to turn on a light or a fan, the Echo performs the task immediately--instead of with a delay while it searched through the router's list of connected devices for the correct one.

The PCs and other devices that use lots of bandwidth (instead of being on standby much of the time) seem to connect faster, and they test (using OOKLA) at significantly faster Internet speeds.

My R7500v2 is broadcasting signals for both bands (2.4 GHz and 5 GHz), and my compatible devices connect with the 5 GHz network whenever I ask them to. However, I don't use the 5 GHz band for anything at present (because it's easiest to have everything that uses a printer on the same band with the printers). Thus I don't know whether the router frequently drops the 5 GHz signal, as other reviewers have stated.

I've used several high-end Linksys routers, and they have performed very well. However, I find that Netgear routers lose their Internet signal far less often, and almost never require rebooting--when Netgear routers need rebooting, the issue is almost always traceable to Comcast problems.

Another reason that I prefer Netgear routers over Linksys routers is that Netgear has no limit (or a very high limit) on the number of devices that you can list by MAC number and tell the router to "allow only these devices to connect to the network". I use this feature as an extra firewall, and find that the Linksys 25-device list is inadequate for my needs.

Finally, the Netgear "Genie" app for managing the router settings is clear and easy to understand. The initial setup for this router is easy, unless you have a nonstandard home network (e.g., my router is connected with the Comcast-supplied equipment in "Bridge" mode), and/or you interrupt the setup routine before it's run through all its steps. If you do land in setup limbo, you can start over by resetting the router to the factory settings (use a paperclip to hold down the reset button for 10-30 seconds--light will blink; unplug from wall for 30 seconds; follow Quick Start instructions again from beginning).
text_fidelity_b: Netgear R7500-200NAS Nighthawk X4 Ultimate Gaming Router - AC2350 4X4 MU-MIMO Dual Band WiFi Gigabit Router (R7500v2) with Open Source Support. Compatible with Amazon Echo/Alexa

text_fidelity_a:
Display Port to HDMI Converter with Audio Adapter I wanted to hear and see Skype on our Sony XBR7 HDMI-only capable 1080p TV, fed from a Lenovo X220 convertable laptop/tablet running System 7 64 bit Ultimate through the DisplayPort. I also wanted to watch some YouTube videos playing from Firefox and hear their audio on my big living room audio system. No such luck.

When first plugged in, I remember briefly seeing the TV via this DisplayPort adapter in the audio device list, but the next time, the TV disappeared and is nowhere to be found. Not in the audio control panel, anyway. It's just gone.

I first chalked this up to the Thinkpad weirdness, as its internal audio card/mic doesn't work with Skype either. If I plug in an external Logitech webcam, it works seamlessly. Internal camera/mic, nothing.

Sony audio problems aside, the video looks great on the big screen, though it overscans a bit and cuts off part of the menu bar at the bottom.

One reviewer said he could see his TV in the list of audio devices and was able to configure its audio to satisfaction. My Sony TV does not show in the Lenovo audio devices list, though it does show as a generic PnP monitor.

I plugged the HDMI cable into a tiny 7" video monitor and whatdayaknow, the audio came through and the device showed up as an audio device. Then I plugged it into a 20" Vizio and sure enough, it works fine too. Same with a Samsung LCD. Three monitors out of four work. The Sony is the only one that doesn't. Hmmmm.

Sooooo, I'm guessing there's something about Sony's DRM or some other HDMI protocol blocking the computer from seeing the TV. I set all the TVs for internal speakers. Routing audio to an external amp is another variable in the equation.

Nothing wrong with the adapter that I can tell, it simply doesn't see certain Sony TV's.
text_fidelity_b: Display Port to HDMI Converter with Audio Adapter

text_fidelity_a:
Garmin 4.3-Inch Carrying Case Bought this for the 750 because it didn't come with a case. A similar (smaller) case came with my 360 and I didn't think this purchase through. After using it and comparing the other cases out there, I would buy a different case.

This slipcase for the 750 fits tight. That's good. The Nuvi won't slip out. But because the 750's on/off switch is now a slider on the top left corner, if you slide it into the case naturally (unit in your right hand, case in your left) the switch rubs against the case. When you pull the unit out, it "automatically" turns on. Thus if you were to pull the unit out partially then push it back in, you could turn it on and not know it.

The solution is to invert the Nuvi so its switch will be at the open end of the case after it's in the case. That way you can see the switch's on/off position and verify it's not on.

More practical issues:

Pros:

- Nicely made: very high quality

- Very compact

- Adequate protection against rattling inside a glove compartment or briefcase

- Good basic case

Cons:

- It can accidentally turn the unit on

- It's black: can't find it easily in the dark buried at the bottom of my shoulder bag when traveling. Experienced this with the 360's case. And if it falls on the floor of a rental car at night, good luck trying to find it. Wish it came in natural leather color.

- Offers no protection while hand holding the unit while walking

The [[ASIN:B0012MI7N2 Garmin Nuvi 800 Series Carrying Case]] case is a wallet style that flips open to reveal the screen. It stays on the unit during use and offers some protection if you dropped your Nuvi on the sidewalk while walking. Downside with that unit appears to be that the cover flap does not latch, allowing the case to flip open in a briefcase and the screen to be scratched by other junk. And it's also black and can get lost on a car floor.

Another alternate is one of the many zippered semi-rigid or neoprene cases.
text_fidelity_b: Garmin 4.3-Inch Carrying Case

text_fidelity_a:
BOSS Audio Systems 625UAB Multimedia Car Stereo - Bluetooth Audio And Hands Free Calling, Single Din, MP3 Player, No CD/DVD Player, USB Port, AUX Input, AM/FM Radio Receiver, Detachable Face This car stereo exceeded all of my expectations. True, those expectations were super low due to how inexpensive this is. But, my goodness, it was nice to get a good surprise for a change.

But then came the bad surprise: one night, we started the car, and the blue lights came on but the stereo did not. It wouldn't turn on. It wouldn't turn off. And when the car sat for a day, it drained the battery dry.

Which fixed it. It needed to have the power cut completely in order to reset. Your mileage may vary, but for me, that's a nonstarter. Get it? The husband thinks it's no big deal, at least not worth replacing until it quits entirely. He's the installer, so he wins.

The sound is perfectly serviceable. It gets loud, and all frequencies are clear. Bluetooth connection works great, though my husband prefers aux in for sound quality (Mr. Ears). It was an easy install in my 2004 Odyssey EX (I bought a wiring harness and a frame kit). Still, I would not buy it again.

Three and a half stars.

text_fidelity_a:
Garmin nüvi 265/265T 3.5-Inch Bluetooth Portable GPS Navigator with Traffic I previously owned a Garmin Nuvi 360 which I loved. I specifically need a GPS that includes Bluetooth, since I use it both for directions and for hands-free phone use (which is rare, but important when I need it). I loved my 360 and used it daily until just a few months ago, when the Bluetooth suddenly stopped working. After troubleshooting with Garmin's tech support, it was determined the unit would need to be sent in for service, and since it was out of warranty, the flat charge for service was $79, which didn't include insured shipping costs.

Well, do the math. Obviously, one can acquire a brand-new GPS for not much more than $79, so I started shopping. That's how I ended up with my new Garmin Nuvi 265T. And I LOVE IT! I'm almost glad that my old unit went on the fritz, because it gave me an excuse to upgrade to this newer, fantastic unit.

The 360 was great for accurate directions, easy to see and read display, and consistent Bluetooth (until it broke). Here's how the 265T is even better:

- Smaller, lighter, and thinner, but with a slightly wider screen.
- No "antenna" on the back to flip up and fiddle with - it just works.
- Uses my existing mount (from ProClips), so no change to that was necessary.
- Includes FREE traffic notifications, which so far seem to work pretty well.
- When you power it on, it seems to bypass the warning screen that you need to "Agree" to quicker, and then shows a simple display: Where To, and View Map. On the 360, if you didn't do anything else, it would sit on the menu indefinitely, but the 265T automatically switches to map display after a few minutes if you don't select anything else. Basically, you can start your car and just forget about it, until you need it!

The traffic feature is ad-supported, so occasionally very small banner-type ads appear on the display, usually offering coupons for local restaurants etc. They are quite small and not intrusive in any way, so I don't mind them. I guess there's also an option to upgrade to a paid traffic service that would not include ads, but I don't see a need for that for my own use.

In general I am thrilled with Garmin products, and this Nuvi 265T is no exception. What a great deal, and a nice early Christmas present for myself!
text_fidelity_b: Garmin nüvi 265/265T 3.5-Inch Bluetooth Portable GPS Navigator with Traffic

text_fidelity_a:
Garmin Nuvi 2595LMT UPDATE: after installing the latest map update and waiting for a very long time for the install software to do its thing and worrying if it had actually finished the install because after about an hour my computer said "the application has unexpectedly quit," the device seems to be working perfectly.

Overall, I like the 2595LMT. It boots and finds the satellites faster and has more information available.

Pros:
1. I can press the lower left "Arrive time" button and change it to a variety of readouts: miles remaining, altitude, time via.
2. Voice command works, mostly, especially on simple commands like "Go Home." More complex commands, like an address, return a wide variety of responses, most of them wrong. (Why it's searching the entire United States when it knows where I am and should be looking locally is beyond me.) I liked the old way of narrowing search to State, then City, then Address. Now it just asks you for the whole address, which it likely doesn't understand.
3. It's slimmer and lighter.
4. Easy to import my favorites from my old Nuvi into the 2595LMT. Using a PC, after plugging the old Nuvi into a computer using the USB port,

a. Navigate until you find the "current.GPX" file on the old Nuvi and
b. Copy it to your desktop (this is also a way to make a backup should you desire.)
c. Rename the file: replace "current" with any word you want, as long as it's not "current") so that it is names "anyword.gpx"
d. Attach the new Nuvi 2595LMT to the computer and navigate until you find the folder with its "current.gpx" file.
e. Copy the "anyword.gpx" file from the desktop into the same folder where the "Current.gpx" file resides.
f. Disconnect and restart. All the old favorites will be added to the current list in your new Nuvi.

5. It doesn't say "recalculating" when you disregard its directions
6. It has lane indicators: a series of arrows in the upper left that tell you which lane to get into to make the next turn. Very cool.
7. Touch screen allows scrolling like a smartphone, at least on some screens.
8. Allows you to add/edit shortcuts like a PC. You can create and move icons around so that you can get to a particular feature with one touch.
9. Micro-SD card only
10. Bigger screen
11. 3-D view of the road
12. Speed limit indicator and simultaneous readout of your actual speed that turns red if you exceed the local speed limit. (I wish it bonged quietly when the speed limit changed to remind you that you have to go slower or can go faster.)

Cons:
1. Sadly, on my unit (even after map and software updates) when I say, "Find Place" it immediately crashes and reboots. And if I say, "Find City" it ignores me, even if I ask it to find New York or Los Angeles. I may try reinstalling the software in case it loaded incompletely for some reason. (UPDATE: I waited a couple of weeks and tried updating the maps again. This time it fully installed and happily all the voice commands now work very well. This alone is a good reason to get is unit. Typing while driving is difficult and dangerous. Voice command is simply wonderful and something I've always wanted in a Garmin.)
2. Stuff has been moved around so that the interface is a bit foreign. For instance, "Favorites" are now "Saved Places" and trying to save or edit a saved place is confusing until you get the hang of it.
3. Doesn't have a powered cradle anymore, only a standard mini-USB on the back. Not a real problem, but it's slower to hook up and remove. I used to be able to drop it on the cradle and go. Now I have to find the end of the cable and thread it into a small port on the back. Minor.
4. The traffic function in my opinion is a joke. Driving LA freeways at most times involves congestion and some delay. It's simply the way it is. The Garmin hates congestion and is constantly trying to get you around it. Thus it's constantly bonging and telling me to get off the freeway to take surface streets, assuming they are magically uncongested when in reality the surface streets during rush hour are ten times worse. I'm pretty much going to ignore its traffic suggestions and may turn it off altogether. If you buy the amazon basics power cord [[ASIN:B003N2POXK AmazonBasics Vehicle Power Cable with Mini-USB Connector for GPS and Other Mini-USB Devices]] it doesn't have a built in traffic receiver and thus defeats the annoying and constant attempts to route you around congestion. Simply put, don't believe the alternate route is going to save you any time. Getting onto surface streets during rush hour is a recipe for even longer delays.
text_fidelity_b: Garmin Nuvi 2595LMT

While my office offered to let me take my monitors home I just didn't have the space, and I do like to occasionally do work at the local cafe or lounge.

Enter this portable screen...
